items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: The interviewee mentions Louis Armstrong only as a comparison for originality ('The only ones that come to my mind is like Armstrong...') and in a historical context ('King Oliver influenced Louis'), with no indication of personal interaction or direct professional relationship.

ctx.x: We know definitely that King Oliver influenced Louis. And others before King Oliver influenced him. It went on down the line, you see. But who did influence Bix with that sound?

Well, I guess a lot of musicians who have played with Hardy, I guess Ray Burt was one that played with him early. But I forgot what interview it was. They were talking about his sound being the pure New Orleans sound, but with a sweet tone that was not characteristic of New Orleans sound. But they say that Buddy Molden, too. But also that Emmett had played in Davenport for a while, and Bix had heard him there. And that he...

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1960-07-14
items.q: I think that's one of the great things about jazz is that you don't have, you don't have to follow the letter on it. It comes out so great. And in fact, Vic's, you know, played a lot of things that were unorthodox, but they came out so, so wonderful. And I guess Louis Armstrong and all the old trump

ctx.x: Do I remember Vic Lebowski? Oh, I took lessons from Vic. After I left Mrs. Asap, as I told you, I began just going out on my own, you know, and learning the jazz tunes and learning how to play jazz. But then after a couple of years I realized that I should improve a little bit on my technique and knowledge of music. So I started taking lessons from Vic, and I took about six months from him, and he really helped me quite a lot. But I never, I just couldn't get away from the unorthodox playing. In fact, Vic used to…
Vic was a kind of a legitimate guy?
